issue.issue_text: Whether Section 142(2)(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, vests jurisdiction for initiating proceedings for an offence under Section 138 in the Court where the cheque is delivered for collection, i.e., through an account in the branch of the bank where the payee or holder in due course maintains an account.

facts: The jurisdiction to try offences for dishonoured cheques under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, has been a contentious issue with evolving legal interpretations.
Initially, in *K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan*, the Supreme Court held that the case could be filed in any of the several locations where a component of the offence occurred.
Later, in *Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod v. State of Maharashtra*, a larger bench restricted the jurisdiction exclusively to the location of the drawee bank (the bank of the person who issued the cheque).
In response to the difficulties caused by the *Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod* judgment, Parliament passed the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act, 2015, which inserted Section 142(2) into the Act.
law: Section 142(2)(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (as amended in 2015) states that an offence under Section 138 shall be tried only by a court within whose local jurisdiction the branch of the bank is situated where the payee (the person receiving the cheque) maintains their account and delivered the cheque for collection.
The Statement of Objects and Reasons for the 2015 Amendment Act explicitly indicates that the insertion of Section 142(2) was a direct consequence of the judgment in *Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod*.
The Supreme Court's decision in *Bridgestone India Private Limited v. Inderpal Singh* affirmed the legal position established by the 2015 amendment.
application: The Court analyzed the legislative intent behind the 2015 amendment, noting that it was specifically enacted to overturn the precedent set in *Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod*.
The Court interpreted the phrase "shall be inquired into and tried only by a Court within whose local jurisdiction..." in Section 142(2) as a clear and mandatory provision.
This language, according to the Court, unambiguously fixes the territorial jurisdiction for a Section 138 offence.
The Court concluded that the new law makes it clear that jurisdiction vests with the court where the payee's bank is located, not the drawer's bank.
The Court also referenced its own subsequent decision in *Bridgestone India*, which had already endorsed and affirmed this new jurisdictional rule.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that Section 142(2)(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, as introduced by the 2015 amendment, decisively vests jurisdiction for initiating proceedings for a Section 138 offence in the court within whose territorial limits the payee's bank branch is located, where the cheque was delivered for collection.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power of the Supreme Court to transfer criminal cases under Section 406 of the Code of Criminal Procedure remains intact in relation to offences under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, notwithstanding the non obstante clause in Section 142(1) of the said Act, if it is found expedient for the ends of justice.
obiter: The insertion of Sections 142(2) and 142-A in the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, was a direct consequence of the judgment of the Supreme Court in Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod vs. State of Maharashtra.

A complaint for an offence under Section 138 must be made within one month of the cause of action, and no court inferior to a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class can try such an offence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Notwithstanding the non-obstante clause in Section 142(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the power of the Supreme Court to transfer criminal cases under Section 406 of the Code of Criminal Procedure remains intact in relation to offences under Section 138 of the Act. The non-obstante clause pertains only to the manner in which cognizance is to be taken for such offences and does not abrogate the Court's transfer powers when it is found expedient for the ends of justice.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied a contextual interpretation to the non-obstante clause in Section 142(1) of the NI Act, holding that the clause must be read and understood in the context and for the purpose it is used, which is to prescribe the procedure for taking cognizance, rather than as a blanket exclusion of other statutes.
The court exercised its power under Section 406 Cr.P.C. based on the standard of whether a transfer is 'expedient for the ends of justice'.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that the non-obstante clause in Section 142 of the NI Act overrides Section 406 Cr.P.C. was rejected. The Court clarified that the clause does not lend itself to the interpretation that Section 406 Cr.P.C. would stand excluded.

The Court held that the non-obstante clause merely dictates the manner in which cognizance is taken for an offence under Section 138 and does not strip the Supreme Court of its power to transfer criminal proceedings.
policy_considerations: When multiple complaint cases pertain to the same transaction, it is advisable to have a common adjudication to obviate the possibility of contradictory findings being rendered by different Courts.
The transfer of cases to a single location was deemed to be convenient and in the interest of all concerned, including the parties and their witnesses.
